title: Salutation to the Timeless
hook: namastvam akaale: salutation to the One beyond time (Jaap, bhujang prayat)

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhujang prayat, the snake's gait, short, long, long, and your line, glide. Did something in your day move smoothly? Today, the first word of the glide. Day three hundred thirty-seven.

Look at your phone's lock screen. What's the biggest thing on it? On a lot of phones, it's the time. Not a photo, not a message. The hour and the minute, huge, in the middle. Calendars, deadlines, birthdays, the slow counting of years in a mirror. So much of a day is measured in time, and every clock is counting something down. Now listen to the first word Jaap Sahib salutes when it starts to glide. Today: salutation to the Timeless.
screen: `THE BIGGEST THING ON YOUR LOCK SCREEN.` → `THE HOUR AND THE MINUTE.` → `EVERY CLOCK COUNTING SOMETHING DOWN.`

segments.voice: The line is namastvam akaale. Namastvam is two words: namah, a bow, a salutation, and tvam, you. A bow to you. Akaale is the One who is akaal. Now open that word. Kaal is time. And in Punjabi and the older languages behind it, kaal also means death, because time is the thing that ends us. Put the small a in front, without, and akaal means without time, and without death. Timeless. Deathless. Both at once. So the very first salutation in the gliding part of Jaap bows to the One who isn't on the clock at all. Sikhs had met this word long before Jaap. In the Mool Mantar, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak calls the One akaal moorat, the form beyond time. Sikhs call God Akal Purakh, the Timeless Being. In Amritsar, beside the Golden Temple, stands the Akal Takht, the Throne of the Timeless, which tradition says the sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind, founded. And the word is in the everyday Sikh greeting: Sat Sri Akal. Truth is the Timeless. A whole theology, folded into hello. Here's what it does on an ordinary day. Every person you love is in time. Your body is in time. Your worries are in time. Jaap's akaal points to something underneath all of it that isn't. Something the clock can't touch. Sikhs bow to that first, before anything else in the glide.
screen: `NAMASTVAM: A BOW TO YOU.` · `KAAL: TIME, AND DEATH.` · `AKAAL: TIMELESS, DEATHLESS.` · `SAT SRI AKAL: TRUTH IS THE TIMELESS.` · then, large: `BEYOND TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say namastvam akaale three times. Slowly, in the snake's rhythm from yesterday. Na-mas-tvam, a-kaa-le. Once. Twice. Three times. Then turn your phone face down, or put the clock out of sight, and sit in the quiet that's left. For these moments, don't count anything, not breaths, not seconds. Just be here, and let time be someone else's job. If you pray, you can rest in the word Akal. The bell holds the time.
Akaal. Without kaal, without time and without death: the Timeless One, the first salutation of Jaap's glide, and the Akal in Sat Sri Akal.
Your line: beyond time. Today, when you glance at the clock in a hurry, let it remind you: not everything is on the clock. Then take one slow breath. Day three hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs greet one another with Sat Sri Akal, call God Akal Purakh, the Timeless Being, and recite namastvam akaale every morning in Jaap Sahib.

original.note: Gurmukhi: akaal, without time and without death; heard daily in Sat Sri Akal.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sat Sri Akal is just how Sikhs say hello.
what it means: it says truth is the Timeless, the same akaal that Jaap bows to first.
what a scholar hears: kaal carries both 'time' and 'death' (Sanskrit kala), so akaal is at once timeless and deathless; it echoes akaal moorat in the Mool Mantar.
